newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian bank merger could be first of many.
newsitem.headline: Austrian bank merger could be first of many.

text.p: Analysts predicted a flurry of takeovers in Austria's crowded financial sector on Monday after two top banks prepared to merge, but they warned Bank Austria's marriage to Creditanstalt could get off to rocky start.

"It is often the case in Europe that where there is one big merger others follow as the competitive environment changes. We have seen it in Holland recently and in Britain," said James Alexander, banking analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.
Market leader Bank Austria succeeded in its 17.2 billion schilling bid for the state's stake in second placed Creditanstalt-Bankverein at the weekend.
The deal will create a financial powerhouse to rank among Europe's top 30 and dominate the domestic scene.

Experts said it would also force other Austrian banks to seek partners to shore up their market position or risk being swept away by a tide of increased competition at the start of a single European currency.

"I expect to see further consolidation leading to no more than three big groups eventually, with the remaining small players allied to a big bank," said Gerhard Auer, analyst at ICE Securities in London.
Austria's more than 4,000 bank branches serve on average only 1,300 people each, putting the country firmly at the bottom of the EU league in terms of branch efficiency.
Bank Austria's sister bank GiroCredit, the nation's third biggest savings bank, and post office bank Postsparkasse (PSK) were both prime takeover targets, analysts agreed.

Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse Bank (First Austrian), disappointed in its bid for Creditanstalt, and the cooperative Raiffeisen group would be waiting in the wings to snap up GiroCredit and PSK, they forecast.

"GiroCredit is in limbo now and we could see a transfer to Die Erste over time," said Mathew Czepliewicz of Salomon Brothers. "And the privatisation of PSK will probably go ahead with Raiffeisen or a combination of Raiffeisen and Die Erste as possible buyers."

The City of Vienna, which controls Bank Austria and GiroCredit through its AVZ foundation, will sell its GiroCredit stake as part of a complicated deal struck by Austria's left-right coalition government. The horse-trading cleared the way for socialist Bank Austria to take over conservative Creditanstalt.
While welcoming the union of the top two banks as a step in the right direction, some analysts said details of the agreement left a lot to be desired.

A clause guaranteeing Creditanstalt's independence for five years and protecting staff from redundancies gave little room to manoeuvre in cutting costs while the imminent privatisation of Bank Austria threatened to open up a new rift in the coalition government, still reeling from the Creditanstalt row.
Doubling up in key areas, like investment banking and east European operations, could rob the new bank of its competitive edge, argued ICE's Auer.

"It is easier to compete with one combined unit that has no clear direction than with two focused businesses," he said. "There is a five year period where basically nothing will change. That takes the commercial logic out of the deal."

This year's sale of the state's 19 percent Bank Austria stake combined with a steady reduction in the City of Vienna's holding could inject new tensions into the fragile coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party, he continued.
"The Creditanstalt chapter has finished and one can only hope that the privatisation of Bank Austria, the placement of new shares plus existing shares, goes more smoothly."
Others were more upbeat and forecast the new bank would eventually realise its full synergy potential.
"There may be some short-term problems in integrating the two operations but five years looks a meaningful target," said Kleinwort's Alexander.
